title: Temperature dependence of a warm ensemble based memory on quantum communication rates
authors: Kenny Gregory, Khaled Mnaymneh, Connor Kupchak, Andrew MacRae
abstract: The success of long-distance quantum communication will hinge on quantum repeater nodes equipped with robust and scalable quantum memories. Such memories must possess specific operating characteristics to make these nodes practical. An attractive option for these memory devices is an atomic warm vapor system operating under the conditions of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). These systems are easy to implement and require relatively low equipment overhead. A key metric in atomic-based quantum memory performance is optical depth, as it is closely tied to the strength of light-matter coupling. Here, we simulate and measure the optical depth-based performance of an EIT quantum memory using a warm atomic vapor cell. We then translate the simulated and measured optical depth and efficiency metrics into expected entanglement distribution rates. Our analysis evaluates the feasibility of these memories in optical quantum repeater nodes, which are essential for robust long-distance quantum communication.
summary: This paper analyzes the feasibility of using warm atomic vapor quantum memories for long-distance quantum communication via quantum repeaters. By simulating and measuring the memory's efficiency dependence on temperature and optical depth, the authors quantify how these physical limitations constrain the achievable entanglement distribution rates. The results provide a crucial tool for designing robust, scalable quantum network nodes.
main_problem: The paper investigates the temperature dependence of quantum memory performance to determine its impact on achievable entanglement distribution rates for long-distance quantum repeaters.
main_result: The analysis provides a framework showing how memory efficiency, which depends on temperature and optical depth, critically limits the overall entanglement rate in quantum repeater nodes.
method: The authors simulate and measure the optical depth-based performance of an EIT quantum memory and translate these metrics into end-to-end entanglement distribution rates using established repeater models.
model_or_system: The system uses a warm atomic vapor cell operating under Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) to function as a quantum memory (QM). The performance is modeled using the entanglement distribution rate equation, incorporating memory efficiency ($\eta_{mem}$) and detector efficiency ($\eta_{det}$).
key_observables: Entanglement distribution rate ($R$), memory efficiency ($\eta_{mem}$), and optical depth ($D$).
important_parameters: Temperature range (328–348 K), attenuation coefficient ($\alpha = 0.2 	ext{ dB/km}$), and node number ($n=2, 4$).
main_assumptions: Assumes the entangled source is maximally entangled, the BSM efficiency is 50%, and initially assumes infinite memory lifetime for model comparisons.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum repeater schematic, the $\Lambda$-system level structure, experimental measurements of optical depth and storage efficiency vs. temperature, and finally, the resulting asynchronous entanglement rate distributions for varying optical depths and node numbers.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the quantum repeater model, then details the physical platform (EIT in warm vapor) and the necessary measurements (optical depth vs. temperature). Finally, it integrates these measured efficiencies into the repeater rate equation to analyze performance trade-offs across different link lengths and node counts.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges atomic physics (EIT, warm vapor dynamics) with quantum networking protocols, providing quantitative metrics (temperature dependence, optical depth scaling) essential for realizing practical quantum communication infrastructure.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Schematic of a quantum repeater scheme where the total length L is divided into n = 3 links. Legend: (BSM) Bell-state measurement, (QM) Quantum memory, (BSS) Bell-state source.

Fig. 2: Optical storage using EIT using optical depths of D = 2, 3, 5 corresponding to simulated optical storage efficiencies of ηmem = 5%, 9%, 16% respectively. In these simulations the control field Rabi frequency was Ωc = 1.5Γ and storage duration of 2µs. Inset: Simulated storage efficiency for increasing optical depths.

Fig. 3: a) Level scheme for 3-level lambda system suitable for optical storage using EIT. b) Schematic diagram of the experimental setup where a single laser is employed for both the control and probe beams. The probe field is frequency modulated at the 87Rb ground state splitting frequency. Both fields are fibre coupled separately into the QMem system and spatially overlapped before propagation inside the gas vapour cell. Glan-laser prisms are used for field combination and separation.

Fig. 5: Asynchronous entanglement rate distributions for varying optical depths used in EIT storage. a) Using experimental optical depths and efficiencies using portable warm vapour QMem system. Distribution rates using theoretical optical depths possible with EIT for b) n = 2 and c) n = 4 links. d) Entanglement rate vs optical depth for different node numbers at a fixed transmission distance of L = 250 km.

Fig. 4: Experimental optical depths and storage efficiencies of the QMem system over temperatures of 328-348K (55-75◦C). The QMem system exhibits an exponential nature for the optical depth and an asymptotic response for the efficiency over the temperatures achievable in our system.
